In the mid/upper-levels, a cyclonic gyre continues to wobble over 
northeastern Canada, with an inverted trough on its western 
periphery that extends westward towards Manitoba. Farther to the 
southwest, the well-advertised shortwave trough originating from 
the exit-region of a Pacific jet extension was quickly moving 
southeastward over the north-central Great Plains. The early stages 
of a large baroclinic leaf associated with this shortwave trough was 
evident on water-vapor imagery, with leading edge of high-level, 
moist ascent advecting into the Ohio River Valley. Throughout the 
next 24-36 hours, these two features will begin to phase, with the 
leading shortwave trough ejecting eastward over the CWA prior to 
dawn Thursday. Several series of shorter-wave perturbations embedded 
within the mean flow will also trail the ejection of the leading 
shortwave trough, as the cyclonic gyre will begin to erode via a 
large-scale wave break over the Pacific Coast. As this occurs, and 
in conjunction with the backside of the amplified trough gradually 
shifting eastward, it will allow a polar surface high currently 
parked in central Nunavut to rotate southward into the region the 
weekend. While the growing season has already ended, there is high 
confidence in a hard freeze this weekend.

At the surface, an ill-defined, quasi-stationary front was draped in 
an east-west-oriented manner across the Ohio River Valley, with the 
tail-end of the front in far southern OH. This front extends much 
farther westward through the Middle Mississippi River Valley before 
bending northwest into eastern NE where a triple point is located 
beneath the shortwave trough aloft. Farther north, a secondary cold 
front of polar origin stems from a surface low in central Ontario, 
and branches southwestward into the Drift Prairie of ND. While these 
two respective frontal systems are far removed from the CWA as of 
this writing, both fronts will cross through the region during the 
next 24-36 hours. The CWA was otherwise bereft of any other surface 
boundary, with a surface high positioned near BNA. Calm winds will 
transition towards the southwest later this morning as the stalled
front in the western part of the CWA undergoes warm-frontogenesis 
and lifts northward in tandem with gradual pressure falls. Today 
will be the last mild day until early next week, and dewpoints 
were lowered through this evening to match the current trends in 
observations. RH values as low as 30 percent are forecast across far 
southern WV and far western VA, but fire weather concerns remain low 
due to the weak transport winds across those locales this afternoon.

The first of two cold fronts will arrive in the western portions of 
the lowlands late tonight, and will be accompanied by a band of 
locally heavy rain showers. Updrafts may reach heights high enough 
to generate lightning, but thermal instability should become 
increasingly slim as the columns saturate amidst moist-adiabatic 
lapse rates. As the leading shortwave trough ejects overhead, it 
will remain open, with any closed cyclone in the mid-levels being 
displaced far to the north of the CWA. Therefore, the primary cold 
front is expected to move through the region in a progressive 
manner and clear the CWA near or prior to sunrise Thursday, with 
the secondary cold front trailing behind. Brisk, northwesterly winds 
are expected post-FROPA due to the modest isallobaric response 
generated by the surface low as it deepens to around 998 mb while 
rotating eastward across far northern WV and southern PA. High 
temperatures for Thursday have also trended cooler from the previous 
assessments, with highs forecast to now peak in the lower 50s across 
the lowlands and the lower-middle 40s in the mountains. Deformation 
banding on the backside of the surface low may eclipse the northern 
counties, with off-and-on rain showers forecast across the lowlands 
during the day Thursday. 

Northwesterly flow advecting in on the backside of the amplifying 
trough will yield an upslope flow event for snow in the mountains 
starting Thursday night and lasting into Sunday morning. The initial 
transition into a rain-snow mix will occur after sunset Thursday, 
with dynamical cooling aiding in a transition to snow during the 
predawn hours Friday. There will be a delay in accumulations of 
snow in the mountains at first, but with wet-bulb temperatures 
falling into the middle 20s by sunrise, accumulations of wet snow 
should begin by sunrise. Farther west into the lowlands, surface 
and wet-bulb temperatures will hover near or slightly below 
freezing, which may result in some pockets of a rain-snow mix or 
possibly some snow Friday morning. However, light precipitation 
rates and warm soil temperatures will prevent any accumulations of 
snow from coming to fruition across those locales. The large-scale
